seg.p: The form σαυνάκα is a hapax legomenon in Aristophanes, appearing only in this passage of the Birds (v. 1038). It is an accusative singular of σαυνάξ, a noun of uncertain etymology and meaning, likely a comic coinage or a dialectal variation for a type of bird or a specific object associated with the bird-cult in the play. Its meaning has been debated: some editors suggest it refers to a 'saw' (σαύρα) due to phonetic similarity, while others propose it denotes a 'squirrel' or a 'magpie', given the context of bird-keeping. The word's obscurity and lack of clear parallels in other comic or tragic texts make it a crux for textual critics and commentators.

seg.head: Line 1629

p.quote: βακταρικροῦσα.

seg.p: The hapax legomenon βακταρικροῦσα (baktarikrousa) is a coined compound adjective describing the bird's sound, blending the root of βᾶκτρος (a type of flute or reed pipe) with κρούω (to strike or sound). The word is a deliberate comic neologism by Aristophanes, likely evoking the shrill, piercing quality of the birds' song to contrast with the human musical tradition, while simultaneously alluding to the satyr play tradition where such grotesque or burlesque sounds were common. Its rarity and the author's specific morphological construction mark it as a key instance of Aristophanic wordplay.

seg.head: Line 1669

p.quote: ἤδη σʼ ὁ πατὴρ εἰσήγαγʼ ἐς τοὺς φράτερας;

seg.p: The accusative plural τοὺς φράτερας refers to the members of a φράτρα (fraternity), a social and religious subdivision of an Athenian deme. In the context of Aristophanic comedy, this term is significant because admission to a φράτρα was a prerequisite for full citizenship and the right to participate in the Assembly. The joke hinges on the absurdity of the character's father having introduced him to this exclusive body, implying a sudden, perhaps illegitimate, elevation to civic status or a satirical take on the ease with which political boundaries could be crossed in the chaotic world of the Birds.

seg.head: Line 1677

p.quote: ἐν τῷ Τριβαλλῷ πᾶν τὸ πρᾶγμα. τί σὺ λέγεις;

seg.p: The phrase 'ἐν τῷ Τριβαλλῷ' (in the Trabelles) functions as an idiom meaning 'completely' or 'totally,' a usage unique to this passage in Aristophanes. The Trabelles (or Triballi) were a Thracian tribe, but here the reference is likely a pun on the Greek word τριβή (tribē), meaning 'friction' or 'rubbing,' suggesting the situation is a 'mess' or 'tangled up.' This wordplay relies on the audience's familiarity with the tribe and the phonetic similarity to the concept of a 'tangled' or 'friction-filled' situation.

seg.head: Line 1679

p.quote: ὄρνιτο παραδίδωμι.

seg.p: The verb παραδίδωμι is here used in a transitive sense with the accusative ὄρνιτο (a rare, possibly poetic or metrical variant of ὄρνιθας) to mean 'deliver up' or 'surrender' the birds, a specific legal or dramatic action central to the plot's resolution where the birds are handed over to the chorus or the protagonist. This usage is distinct from the more common intransitive or passive forms and requires the accusative of the thing delivered.

seg.head: Line 1681

p.quote: εἰ μὴ † βαδίζειν † ωἅσπερ αἱ χελιδόσιν λέγει.

seg.p: The transmitted text is corrupt and widely recognized as a crux. The phrase 'βαδίζειν' (to walk) makes little sense in the context of birds, and the dative 'χελιδόσιν' (to swallows) lacks a governing preposition or verb of motion compatible with 'βαδίζειν'. Most editors, following the suggestion of Hermann and others, conjecture that 'βαδίζειν' should be replaced with 'πετοῦν' (to fly) or that the verb is missing entirely, with 'ὡσπερ' introducing a comparison to the flight of swallows. The phrase 'λέγει' (says) is also problematic here; some suggest it is a corruption of 'ἕπει' (follows) or that the sentence is a fragment of a larger dialogue where the verb is elliptical. The current text as transmitted is syntactically and semantically incoherent without significant emendation.

seg.head: Line 1730

p.quote: αὐτὸν καὶ τὴν Βασίλειαν.

seg.p: The phrase 'τὴν Βασίλειαν' is an elliptical construction where the substantive noun is omitted. In this context, 'Βασίλειαν' functions as a substantive adjective referring to 'τὴν Βασίλειαν πόλιν' (the royal city) or, more likely given the play's plot, 'τὴν Βασίλειαν ἀρχήν' (the royal power/kingdom). This usage relies on the audience's immediate recognition of the specific political entity being established by the birds, rather than the standard grammatical expectation of an explicit noun following a definite article and adjective. The omission serves a rhetorical purpose, emphasizing the abstract concept of sovereignty as a tangible object to be possessed alongside the protagonist.

seg.head: Line 1739

p.quote: ηὔθυνε παλιντόνους,

seg.p: The verb αὐθύνειν (here ἠύθυνε) in this context denotes 'to steer' or 'to guide' a vessel, but the construction with the accusative object παλιντόνους (literally 'those with reversed rudders' or 'those steering backward') is a striking example of Aristophanic wordplay. The adjective παλίντονος is rare and likely coined for the comic effect of the birds' chaotic flight, suggesting a deliberate inversion of the normal direction of travel. The use of the aorist ἠύθυνε indicates a specific, completed action within the narrative flow, contrasting with the ongoing or habitual nature of the birds' flight described elsewhere in the play.
